metadata.title: Social inequality in digital competencies among students in Germany: A trend analysis using ICILS data 2013-2023

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the German samples from ICILS 2013, 2018, and 2023, which are based on a multi-stage clustered sampling design (schools, then students and teachers within schools). For the achievement component (computer and information literacy, CIL), the authors apply student-level weighting factors provided in the ICILS dataset to account for unit non-response. Because the analysis is clustered at the school level, they additionally compute cluster-robust standard errors at school level in Stata (vce(cluster)), and they report multilevel robustness checks. The manuscript does not name a specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that analyses are weighted using the student-level weighting factors from the dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses the German ICILS samples for 2013, 2018, and 2023 (computer-based assessment of computer and information literacy, CIL) and restricts to regular schools. From the full German sample across the three time points (10,945 students), the authors further restrict to students aged 14–16 (8th grade age band) and report an analytic sample of 8,548 cases. For the achievement outcome, they use the ICILS plausible value approach (five plausible values per student) and perform multiple imputation for item non-response using MICE, integrating results across 30 imputed datasets via Rubin’s rules. Analyses are conducted with weighted estimation and cluster-robust standard errors at the school level; multilevel models are used as a robustness check.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2013-2023 Germany Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Trend/descriptive: SES gap increases from 43 to 66 competence points (p < 0.001). SD-based gap increases from 15.9 to 25.0 competence points per SD of ISEI (p < 0.001). Correlation changes: books-at-home gap increases from 66 to 86 competence points (χ2 = 5.4; p < 0.05); upper-track gap increases from ~65 to >85 competence points (χ2 = 6.2; p < 0.05). KHB decomposition: digital home environment contribution ~1 competence point (≈5–6% relative) and stable; cultural home environment absolute contribution 4.4 to 5.5 competence points (relative ~26% stable); school environment absolute contribution 9.9 to 12.4 competence points (relative 60% to 58%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2013-2023 Germany Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) the study examined how parental SES relates to students’ digital competencies over time and found that the SES gap widened significantly from 2013 to 2023 (from 43 to 66 competence points; and from 15.9 to 25.0 competence points per SD of ISEI). This indicates that strengthening compensatory supports for low-SES students’ cultural and school learning conditions may be necessary to prevent widening digital inequality, though the study is observational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes the German ICILS trend data for 2013, 2018, and 2023 (8th-grade students aged 14–16) using the computer-based CIL achievement scale (210–708 points) and plausible values (five PVs per student). The authors restrict to regular schools and apply student-level ICILS weights, multiple imputation for item non-response via MICE (30 imputed datasets), and Rubin’s rules to combine PV-based estimates; they also use cluster-robust standard errors at the school level. Across the period, average digital competencies decline, but socioeconomic disparities increase: the SES gap rises from 43 to 66 competence points (p < 0.001) and from 15.9 to 25.0 competence points per SD of ISEI (p < 0.001). The strongest changing associations are for the cultural home environment (books at home) and school track (upper secondary), while the digital home environment shows stable, small explanatory contribution in KHB decomposition. Limitations include reliance on observational trend comparisons and simplified measurement of cultural and school environments (e.g., books at home only).
